name: Bahonsuai
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Primary: Mead, David E. 1998. Proto-Bungku-Tolaki: reconstruction of its phonology and aspects of its morphosyntax. PhD dissertation, Rice University (Rice repository handle 1911/19290; scanned copy, 534 pp.), sec. 3.1.2 'Syllable patterns and stress', p. 97; scope table naming Bahonsuai on p. 93. Secondary: Mead, David E. 1999. The Bungku-Tolaki languages of south-eastern Sulawesi, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-91. Canberra: RSPAS, ANU (sealang.net PL scan), Appendix 3 'Selected word lists', transcription convention (g), p. 101; Bahonsuai word list BAH (list no. 34) pp. 103ff; language entry p. 54.
catalog_locator: Mead 1998 p. 97, sec. 3.1.2 'Syllable patterns and stress'; scope table p. 93. Mead 1999 pp. 101-102, Appendix 3, convention (g) and long-vowel/syllable remarks; BAH word-list rows pp. 103ff. (47 BAH-labelled lines, no stress marks).
catalog_quote: Mead 1998:97 (sec. 3.1.2 Syllable patterns and stress): "I assume that in Proto–Bungku-Tolaki stress fell on the penultimate syllable, there being no reason to reconstruct otherwise. All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages also exhibit penultimate stress." Mead 1998:93: "Data for all of them are limited to lists of 226 words collected under field survey conditions. ... In particular the reader may assume that unless otherwise noted: sound changes discussed for Mori Bawah, Wawonii and Bungku likewise apply to Bahonsuai, Koroni and Taloki" [first row of a three-column table; rows 2-3: Mori Atas -> Tomadino; Tolaki -> Waru, Rahambuu and Kodeoha]. Mead 1999:101-102 (Appendix 3, Selected word lists, incl. Bahonsuai): "(g) In the absence of any stress marking, one can assume penultimate stress occurring on the next to last written vowel. ... (d) None of the Bungku-Tolaki languages have phonemically long vowels. Phonetically long vowels are nearly always a reflection of two vowels of the same quality, and have been transcribed as such in the following data ... All of the Bungku-Tolaki languages may be considered open syllable languages, with the only syllable patterns being V and CV."
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: I assume that in Proto–Bungku-Tolaki stress fell on the penultimate syllable, there being no reason to reconstruct otherwise. All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages also exhibit penultimate stress.
new_statements.citation: Mead, David E. 1998. Proto-Bungku-Tolaki: reconstruction of its phonology and aspects of its morphosyntax. PhD dissertation, Rice University.
new_statements.locator: sec. 3.1.2 'Syllable patterns and stress', p. 97 (p. 114); Bahonsuai named as a Bungku-Tolaki language on p. 94 (p. 111)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: rendered page scan (Mead 1998 printed p. 97 = p. 114 of, 534 pp.) reads exactly "I assume that in Proto–Bungku-Tolaki stress fell on the penultimate syllable, there being no reason to reconstruct otherwise. All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages also exhibit penultimate stress." immediately before heading "3.1.3 Distribution of phonemes"; the scanned file lines 344-348 carries the same sentences (dash rendered as em-dash by scanned). Section 3.1.2 (p. 96-97) also reconstructs V(C)/CV(C) syllables with codas only word-finally; nothing on secondary stress or exceptions. Scope check: scanned p. 93-94 (pp. 110-111) says the minor languages known only from 226-item survey lists are…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word in every present-day Bungku-Tolaki language, Bahonsuai included; the companion survey volume (Mead 1999: 101) prints the Bahonsuai wordlist under the convention that unmarked words have penultimate stress on the next-to-last written vowel, and no Bahonsuai item is marked otherwise.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Mead 1999: 101-102 notes that only V and CV syllables occur, that there are no phonemic long vowels, and that a 'prestress' lengthened vowel can reflect a reduced vowel sequence (examples from Tolaki, not Bahonsuai).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, from citation forms in a 226-item survey wordlist (Bahonsuai list no. 34, elicited by Mead 09 Jan 1989); the deciding sentence is a family-wide generalisation over all Bungku-Tolaki languages, not a Bahonsuai-specific phonological description.
new_statements.identity_note: Statement is family-level: Mead 1998 covers 'all present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages' and names Bahonsuai (baho1237) among them (p. 94); Mead 1999 prints the Bahonsuai wordlist (BAH, no dialects reported, village of Bahonsuai, Bungku Tengah) under a penultimate-stress default with no marked exceptions. No Bahonsuai-specific phonology exists; catalog entry should be flagged 'family-wide statement by the fieldworker who collected the Bahonsuai list', closest relative Mori Bawah (mori1268 group).

Bahonsuai is listed on p. 94 (p. 111) among the minor languages known only from a 226-item survey list and grouped with Mori Bawah for sound changes.

sources.citation: Mead, David E. 1999. The Bungku-Tolaki languages of south-eastern Sulawesi, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-91. Canberra: RSPAS, Australian National University. xi+188 pp.
sources.note: Appendix 3 'Selected word lists', p. 101 (p. 113, page scan verified), phonemicisation convention (g): 'In the absence of any stress marking, one can assume penultimate stress occurring on the next to last written vowel.' The Bahonsuai list (BAH; list no. 34, speaker Ridwan, Bahonsuai village, elicited 09 Jan 1989 by D. Mead, rated 'very good', p. 96-98) is one of the 27 lists printed, and none of its 47 rows in the text carries a stress mark (p. 103 image checked). Language entry for Bahonsuai on p. 54 (p. 66) covers classification, location, use; no phonology section for the language itself…
